addressed_problems.content: The mechanistic basis for lottery ticket transferability across tasks remains unresolved. Although bespoke lottery ticket masks share a small consistent core of unpruned parameters and can be retrained on related image classification tasks, the underlying reasons why these shared parameters suffice for transfer are not characterized—whether they implement generic feature extractors, preserve information pathways, or bias optimization is unknown.

Whether the iterative pruning and rewinding procedure for finding trainable sparse sub-networks (lottery tickets) scales to larger models and datasets, such as ResNet-50 on ImageNet, remains an open problem. Prior work and this study note difficulties in producing trainable small sparse tickets in such regimes, and the factors limiting scalability are not understood.

It is not established whether the proposed consensus intersection method for generating prêt-à-porter lottery tickets generalizes to large-scale regimes (e.g., ImageNet-scale tasks) without further methodological adaptation. The method has been demonstrated only on smaller architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG11, ResNet18) and datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, KMNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN), leaving its applicability to larger models and more complex tasks an open question.

The sensitivity of lottery ticket retrainability to training protocol and hyperparameters is a recognized limitation. Failures observed on certain datasets (e.g., SVHN in these experiments) indicate that dataset-specific training recipes or optimizer schedules can materially affect ticket retrainability, and the optimal training regimes for consensus-derived prêt-à-porter tickets have not been determined.

The optimal number and choice of source tasks for constructing prêt-à-porter lottery tickets via mask intersection remain unresolved. It is unclear how many tasks should be included and whether task similarity or diversity affects the quality of the resulting consensus mask.

The optimal threshold of agreement for constructing prêt-à-porter lottery tickets (intersection vs. k-out-of-N voting) is an open empirical question. While this work uses strict intersection, other thresholds may yield better trade-offs between sparsity and generality, and the impact of the threshold on ticket performance has not been systematically studied.

The choice of pruning rule used to source the bespoke lottery tickets that are intersected to form prêt-à-porter tickets is a methodological design choice that remains unresolved. Different pruning techniques (e.g., global unstructured, structured magnitude-based) produce different masks, and it is not known which pruning rule yields the most effective consensus mask.

A theoretical characterization of what distinguishes a lottery ticket mask from other sub-networks (beyond empirical measures of retrainability and mask overlap) is missing. Principled importance definitions and analytic explanations for the observed mask structure and variance properties are lacking, leaving the fundamental nature of winning tickets unexplained.

Modern deep learning uses heavily over-parametrized neural networks that often contain sparse sub-networks able to be trained to competitive accuracy (the "lottery ticket" phenomenon). Prior practice for discovering such sub-networks relies on an iterative, magnitude-based pruning pipeline: train a dense model for some epochs, prune a small fraction of lowest-magnitude parameters, rewind or reinitialize the remaining weights, and repeat many sequential pruning iterations. This procedure has three empirically important shortcomings that motivate the present work. First, the magnitude-based importance proxy and the iterative pipeline are noisy and unstable: stochasticity in training, underconstrained weights in over-parameterized models, and slow convergence of weight magnitudes can cause misranking of important parameters, necessitating many cautious, sequential pruning iterations to avoid destroying trainable sub-networks. Second, the community lacks a principled understanding of whether the sparse "winning" sub-network is unique within a given initialization and architecture, and whether different pruning algorithms or different source tasks identify the same or different trainable sub-networks. This gap limits interpretation of what a lottery ticket represents and whether multiple distinct, comparably-performing sparse solutions coexist. Third, the iterative pruning workflow is inherently sequential and computationally expensive to apply at scale or across multiple source tasks: finding a high-sparsity ticket typically requires many rounds of train-prune-rewind, which raises practical barriers for parallelization and rapid ticket sourcing. These limitations jointly prevent principled, parallel, and computationally efficient identification of compact, trainable sub-networks and obstruct explanations for observed transferability of tickets across related tasks.

nodes.content: The lottery ticket hypothesis posits existence of sparse, trainable sub-networks inside over-parametrized models, but prior empirical practice typically reports a single ticket found by one chosen pruning pipeline and leaves open whether that ticket is unique. If lottery tickets were unique, different pruning algorithms or repeated runs with the same initialization would converge to essentially the same mask; if not, then the conceptual role of a ticket as "the" sparse backbone is ambiguous. Existing studies did not systematically compare mask structure across a diverse set of pruning rules while controlling for initialization, so it remained unclear whether different importance proxies or algorithmic choices merely produce equivalent masks in structure (differing only in e.g. exact weight values) or whether they find genuinely different sparse connectivity patterns. Without this knowledge, conclusions about the nature of critical pathways, the interpretability of identified masks, and the generality of pruning-based importance measures are incomplete.

Transferability of lottery tickets—retraining a ticket discovered on one dataset on a different dataset—has been reported but without a clear, quantitative account of how similar the underlying masks are across tasks. If bespoke masks were nearly identical across tasks, transferability could be explained simply by mask overlap; if they were dissimilar, transfer must rely on other mechanisms. Prior work did not measure per-layer and total mask overlap across many task pairs while holding initialization fixed, leaving unresolved whether transfer stems from near-identity of masks or from a small shared sub-network plus task-specific variations. This uncertainty hampers understanding of what components of a ticket are general-purpose versus task-specialized.

The standard iterative magnitude-based ticket-finding pipeline is sequential and computationally costly because it relies on many rounds of cautious pruning to avoid eliminating important parameters. Moreover, magnitude-based rankings are noisy, so many iterations are used to mitigate risk of permanently removing critical connections. There is therefore a practical need for a principled procedure that reduces the required number of sequential iterations while preserving trainability of the resulting sparse sub-network. A consensus-based intersection across bespoke tickets addresses this need by exploiting the hypothesis that parameters consistently retained across multiple tasks are more reliably important; this approach has not been empirically evaluated as an alternative to long sequential pruning runs, nor has its ability to preserve trainability while enabling parallel sourcing been demonstrated before this work.

The lottery ticket discovery literature uses different post-pruning weight-handling strategies (rewinding to initialization, rewinding to an early checkpoint, or finetuning the remaining weights) but the degree to which this choice influences the connectivity structure of the final mask has not been systematically quantified across pruning techniques. This is important because such methodological choices affect reproducibility, interpretation of which connections are "important," and whether conclusions about ticket structure depend on weight-handling conventions rather than intrinsic network properties. Without this quantification, comparisons across studies that use different weight-handling protocols are difficult to interpret.

Different pruning criteria prioritize different importance proxies (per-channel norms, per-parameter magnitudes, global magnitude ranking, etc.), but practitioners lack quantitative guidance on which criterion is most likely to identify a task-generalizable core of parameters across related tasks. This choice matters when one wants to source tickets for transfer or produce a consensus ticket by intersecting per-task masks: a pruning rule that produces more consistent per-weight retention across tasks will yield larger intersections and thus denser consensus backbones. Prior work compared pruning rules for accuracy-sparsity trade-offs but did not directly evaluate consistency of per-weight selection across tasks with identical initialization.

The initial scale and distribution of weights that constitute a sparse sub-network influence training dynamics and stability, and prior explanations of lottery ticket retrainability focused on the importance of initialization values for winning tickets. However, it was not known whether consensus-derived tickets would inherit favorable initialization statistics or whether intersecting bespoke masks would disproportionately select weights with different initialization properties. Establishing that consensus masks concentrate on weights with smaller initial variance clarifies a potential mechanism for why consensus tickets remain trainable despite high sparsity and supports the use of consensus as a denoising procedure for importance selection.

Recent work on "supermasks" and lottery tickets raised the question whether a mask alone (applied to a random initialization) can already encode predictive structure before any training. The practical and theoretical implications differ: an above-random supermask at initialization suggests the mask itself encodes a good solution, while lack of such performance indicates training dynamics remain essential. Previous reports were mixed and often limited to specific models; a systematic account across multiple architectures and tasks was needed to clarify whether mask-at-initialization performance is generally present or exceptional.

Applying any of the following iterative pruning techniques—global unstructured magnitude pruning, $L_1$-based unstructured magnitude pruning, $L_2$-based structured magnitude pruning, $L_\infty$-based structured magnitude pruning, random structured pruning, and random unstructured pruning—to replicas of the same base neural network with identical random initialization, and following the experimental training/pruning protocol used here (stochastic gradient descent for 30 epochs per pruning round, constant learning rate 0.01, batch size 32, 20% of remaining parameters pruned per iteration, and rewinding unpruned weights to their initialization before the next iteration), yields multiple distinct sparse sub-networks that retrain to comparable test accuracy at similar overall sparsity levels on the evaluated image-classification datasets (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, Kuzushiji-MNIST, EMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN) and architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG11, ResNet18).  Here a binary mask m over the D parameters θ is defined by m_i = 1 if parameter θ_i is retained (unpruned) and 0 if pruned, and structural dissimilarity between two masks m1 and m2 is measured by the Jaccard distance d_J(m1,m2) = 1 - |m1 ∩ m2| / |m1 ∪ m2|; in the reported experiments both per-layer and total Jaccard distances between masks found by different pruning rules increase as pruning iterations proceed (often approaching maximal dissimilarity), demonstrating that the same initialization/architecture can contain multiple, different trainable sparse solutions rather than a single unique winning ticket.

metadata.narrative: The combination of multi-method mask-distance measurements (H1) and comparable accuracy curves across pruning rules (H2) produces strong evidence that different pruning procedures produce structurally distinct yet trainable sub-networks from the same initialization. The dominant residual risk is measurement: Jaccard distance documents set-level dissimilarity but does not by itself prove functional non-equivalence (P1). A secondary, protocol-dependence risk (P2) exists because hyperparameter choices could amplify divergence; however, the across-method, across-seed consistency reported in the paper meaningfully mitigates that risk, leaving the conclusion well supported within the evaluated regimes.

nodes.title: Multiple distinct trainable sparse sub-networks arise from different pruning rules

nodes.content: When identical replicas of the same base architecture and identical initialization are each pruned using the same pruning procedure to produce task-specific (bespoke) masks, the pairwise structural dissimilarity between bespoke masks sourced on different datasets grows with overall sparsity: measuring masks m as binary indicators of retained parameters and using the Jaccard distance d_J(m1,m2) = 1 - |m1 ∩ m2| / |m1 ∪ m2|, the experiments on the considered image-classification datasets and architectures show that pairwise Jaccard distances increase as sparsity increases and can approach near-disjointness at extreme sparsities.  Nonetheless, even at very high sparsity (for example, ≈99% overall sparsity observed for LeNet in these experiments) bespoke masks retain a small but consistent shared backbone of unpruned parameter indices, quantified in the reported results as roughly 6–10% of the unpruned parameters overlapping across tasks.

metadata.narrative: The paper supplies direct, quantitative measurements of inter-task overlap (H3) and transfer performance (Fig. 6) to support that bespoke masks are largely dissimilar yet share a small core. The main load-bearing uncertainty is causal/interpretive: while the observed ~6–10% shared backbone (H3) is real, it is not proven that this small core is the mechanism enabling transfer (P3); moreover, the reported overlap magnitude depends on pruning-rule and threshold choices (P4). These uncertainties narrow the claim from a mechanistic explanation to a descriptive one about measured overlap, but do not negate the empirical observation of a small consistent core across the tested tasks.

nodes.title: Bespoke masks across source tasks are largely dissimilar but retain a small shared backbone

nodes.content: Constructing a consensus mask by taking the element-wise intersection (logical AND) of multiple low-to-moderate-sparsity bespoke binary masks obtained from identical initializations but trained on different source tasks produces a high-sparsity consensus mask that is itself a trainable sub-network: in the reported experiments the bespoke masks were obtained via global unstructured magnitude pruning with rewinding after T = 2 pruning iterations at 20% per iteration on N = 5 source image-classification tasks (MNIST, FashionMNIST, KMNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN) using identical training hyperparameters (SGD 30 epochs per iteration, learning rate 0.01, batch size 32), and the intersection of those five bespoke masks produced a prêt-à-porter mask with sparsity around 85% for LeNet (comparable to the sparsity of a bespoke mask obtained after nine sequential pruning iterations); when the resulting intersection mask was retrained under the same training protocol it reached test accuracies comparable to bespoke tickets of similar sparsity.  Because each bespoke mask used to build the intersection can be obtained independently on separate machines, this intersection-based procedure parallelizes the sourcing stage and therefore reduces elapsed wall-clock time by avoiding extra sequential pruning iterations, while not reducing the total CPU work required to produce the same number of pruning iterations.

metadata.narrative: Empirical results show that intersecting N=5 low-sparsity bespoke masks yields high-sparsity prêt-à-porter masks that retrain to similar accuracy under the authors' protocol (H4), and the construction is formally parallelizable and instantiated in Alg. 1 (H5). The principal vulnerabilities are (a) sensitivity to the limited retraining protocol used to measure comparability (P5) — parity might shift under different tuning or longer schedules — and (b) the practical runtime benefit claim lacks direct wall-clock measurements (P6). Consequently, the claim that intersection yields trainable, high-sparsity tickets is credible in the evaluated setting, while operational speedup statements should be treated as algorithmic potential rather than empirically measured runtime gains.

nodes.title: Prêt-à-porter tickets via mask intersection yield high-sparsity, trainable consensus sub-networks

nodes.content: The choice of how to handle weights after each pruning iteration—either rewinding unpruned weights to their initial values prior to the next training round or finetuning the pruned network in place—materially changes the masks produced by subsequent pruning iterations: using binary masks m as indicators of retained parameters and the Jaccard distance d_J(m1,m2) = 1 - |m1 ∩ m2| / |m1 ∪ m2| to compare masks, finetuning-in-place yields masks that are significantly different from masks produced under rewinding, and the Jaccard distance between masks produced by the two strategies grows as pruning progresses in the experiments reported here (training/pruning rounds each consisting of 30 SGD epochs, 20% pruning per iteration).  For magnitude-based structured pruning rules the observed growth of Jaccard divergence with pruning iteration is approximately logarithmic in the experimental plots, whereas magnitude-based unstructured pruning produces more complex, layer-dependent divergence trends.

metadata.narrative: Layer-resolved Jaccard analyses (H6) consistently show that finetuning versus rewinding produces divergent masks across pruning iterations and pruning schemes, providing a robust empirical basis for Conclusion 4. The remaining uncertainty is whether the magnitude and pattern of divergence generalize to all finetuning schedules (P7); nonetheless, the reported systematic trends across methods and seeds indicate that weight-handling choice is a substantive, reproducible factor shaping mask structure.

nodes.title: Weight handling (rewind vs finetune) substantially changes subsequent mask structure

nodes.content: Using as a consistency statistic the count of weights that remain unpruned in k out of the considered tasks (k ∈ {0,…,5}) across five image-classification tasks (MNIST, FashionMNIST, KMNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN), global unstructured $L_1$-based magnitude pruning was the pruning rule that most often left the same parameter indices unpruned across multiple tasks in the experiments reported here: that is, under global unstructured pruning a larger fraction of weights were observed to be commonly retained across tasks than under the other magnitude-based structured or layer-wise criteria tested, when measured by the number of commonly unpruned weights per k-bin; this comparison excludes the trivial consistency of deterministically-seeded random pruning baselines, which reproduce the same mask by construction.

metadata.narrative: Figure 12's cross-task tallies (H7) supply concrete evidence that global unstructured pruning, in the evaluated experiments, preserves the same parameter indices across multiple tasks more often than the other magnitude-based criteria tested, justifying the conclusion's comparative claim. The main caveat is metric-dependence (P8): raw counts can be biased by layer sizes and the exclusion of trivial random baselines is necessary; alternative normalized or function-weighted metrics might alter the ranking. Within the paper's chosen metric and setting, the conclusion is supported.

nodes.title: Global unstructured magnitude pruning most consistently preserves the same weights across tasks (excluding deterministic random baselines)

nodes.content: In the experiments reported here the subset of parameters that survive into prêt-à-porter consensus masks tend to have initial values whose empirical standard deviation, averaged per layer, is smaller than the empirical standard deviation of the initial values of parameters that survive in bespoke masks of comparable sparsity: for each layer the paper reports the average empirical standard deviation of initialized weights over four subsets (the full layer, the prêt-à-porter subset, the CIFAR-10 bespoke subset, the MNIST bespoke subset), and the prêt-à-porter subsets show smaller layer-wise standard deviations than bespoke subsets; this smaller-initial-variance property of the weights selected by the intersection correlates with improved retrainability and training stability in the reported retraining experiments (i.e., better behaved learning curves and more stable optimization under the fixed training recipe used).

metadata.narrative: The paper documents that prêt-à-porter-selected weights exhibit smaller per-layer empirical standard deviation at initialization (H8) and correlates this statistic with better retrainability shown elsewhere (H4). The primary load-bearing uncertainty is causal: the paper presents correlational evidence but no targeted intervention demonstrating that smaller variance causes improved learnability (P9). Thus, the observed statistical regularity is credible and suggestive of a denoising mechanism, but the causal attribution remains provisional pending controlled manipulations.

nodes.title: Prêt-à-porter masks concentrate on parameters with smaller initial variance correlated with better retrainability

nodes.content: Evaluating bespoke and prêt-à-porter binary masks at initialization (i.e., applying the mask to the network with no further training) under the preprocessing and resizing procedures used in these experiments (images normalized to training-set statistics, resized to the input size expected by each architecture, and, for ResNet/VGG/AlexNet, resized to (224,224,3); for LeNet resized to (28,28,1)), and using up to six random seeds, the majority of mask-architecture-task combinations yield test performance no better than random guessing; the reported exceptions are bespoke masks sourced on large, highly over-parameterized architectures such as AlexNet and VGG11, which in some runs exhibited non-trivial initial performance.  Some runs are missing for certain architecture/dataset pairs as noted in the experimental log, so these initialization results pertain to the tested architectures, datasets, and seeds in the reported experiments.

metadata.narrative: The authors systematically evaluated masks at initialization across architectures and datasets (H9) and found that only large, over-parameterized architectures sometimes yield above-random supermask performance. The main limitation is sampling and some missing seeds noted in the appendices (P10), so the negative finding is best read as robust within the evaluated experimental regime rather than a universal law. Given the transparency about missing runs and the cross-architecture pattern, the conclusion is reasonably well supported for the studied settings.

nodes.title: Most masks are not above-random at initialization except for large, over-parameterized models

nodes.content:
Let a binary mask m over a network with D parameters θ be defined by m_i = 1 iff parameter θ_i is unpruned and m_i = 0 iff θ_i is pruned; given two such masks m1 and m2 defined on the same architecture and identical initialization, their structural overlap is quantified by the Jaccard distance d_J(m1,m2) = 1 - |m1 ∩ m2| / |m1 ∪ m2|, where |·| denotes set cardinality of indices with value 1; this set-theoretic measure captures only which parameter indices are commonly retained or pruned and therefore does not by itself establish that the two resulting masked networks compute different input-output functions after retraining, nor does it rule out equivalence up to permissible reparameterizations such as permutation symmetries of neurons, global sign flips of weights, or layer-wise reparameterizations that leave the function class invariant.
      Fig.3, Fig.4, Fig.10

metadata.failure_mode: If the Jaccard metric fails to detect that many high-d_J mask pairs are functionally equivalent under reparameterizations or produce indistinguishable predictor functions when retrained, then the conclusion that "a single initialization/architecture can contain multiple, different trainable sparse solutions" would be narrowed: the empirical observation would reduce to "different pruning rules select different index sets" without implying distinct, irreducible trainable solutions, and the interpretive claim about multiplicity of winning tickets would be unsupported. The intermediate step that breaks is the paper's mapping from mask structural dissimilarity (Fig. 3, Fig. 4, Fig. 10) to claim of distinct trainable subnetworks; without functional divergence evidence, the implication from d_J ≈ 1 to distinct solutions fails, leaving only the narrower claim about mask-set differences.
metadata.weakness_reason: Jaccard is a clear, interpretable measurement of mask overlap, but the paper's central claim in Conclusion 1 is about the non-uniqueness of "winning" tickets as trainable solutions. If structurally different masks nevertheless define functionally equivalent (or interchangeable via simple symmetries) sub-networks when retrained, then demonstrating high d_J alone does not prove there are multiple distinct winning tickets in the sense of different trainable solutions. Establishing genuine multiplicity requires functional/representational divergence tests (e.g., distinct learned functions, different validation trajectories, inability to map parameters by symmetry) beyond set overlap.

nodes.title: Jaccard distance measures set overlap but not functional distinction

nodes.content:
The reported divergences between masks found by different pruning methods were obtained under a fixed experimental protocol in these experiments—training with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for 30 epochs per pruning round, constant learning rate 0.01, batch size 32, pruning 20% of remaining connections per iteration, and rewinding unpruned weights to their initialization between pruning iterations—run with six random seeds on a collection of vision datasets and architectures (LeNet, AlexNet, VGG11, ResNet18); the particular choice of these hyperparameters (training length per iteration, constant learning rate, per-iteration pruning fraction, rewinding schedule), the number of pruning iterations carried out, and the selection of datasets and architectures affect the noisiness of magnitude-based importance rankings and therefore influence how and how quickly masks diverge under different pruning rules.
      Sections 3 and 4 (training protocol and pruning hyperparameters)

metadata.failure_mode: If divergence across pruning methods is primarily a product of the chosen training/pruning hyperparameters (for example, short pre-prune training, aggressive 20% steps, or rewinding policy), then changing to other reasonable protocols (longer pre-prune convergence, different pruning fractions, different rewind checkpoints) could reduce mask differences and the conclusion would overstate general non-uniqueness. The intermediate break is that the observed d_J growth (Figs. 3/4/10) would no longer be robust; the conclusion would be narrowed to "under these pipeline settings, different pruning rules produce different masks" rather than a general statement about architectures/initializations.

refs.text: Sections 3 and 4 (training protocol and pruning hyperparameters)

metadata.weakness_reason: The paper controls many variables, but the choice of a single modest training recipe (30 epochs, constant LR, 20% per-iteration pruning) and the specific rewinding policy are themselves modeling choices that affect weight-magnitude dynamics and pruning sensitivity. If mask divergence is sensitive to these choices, then the conclusion about non-uniqueness may be contingent on the pipeline rather than a general property of the initialization/architecture pair.

nodes.title: Experimental hyperparameters and scope can influence mask divergence

nodes.content:
The reported 6–10% overlap of unpruned parameter indices across bespoke masks at extreme sparsity levels is a set overlap statistic: treating each bespoke mask as the set of retained parameter indices and computing the fraction of indices that are retained across tasks measures only index-level agreement and does not by itself prove that the small shared set of retained indices is the causally sufficient component that confers transferability or that the task-specific retained parameters are not the dominant determinants of retrainability on any particular target task.
      Fig.5

metadata.failure_mode: If the 6–10% shared core were not the causal substrate for transfer but merely a correlated residual (e.g., because retrainability depends on different, larger patterns or on optimization dynamics influenced by other weights), then the claim that bespoke masks "share a small consistent core" would remain true as a descriptive statistic but would not justify the implied explanatory link to transfer. The chain from measured overlap (Fig. 5) to explanation of transferability would break: transfer claims would need additional causal evidence (ablations / retrain-from-core experiments) to remain supported.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper documents a small consistent backbone by intersection counts, but concluding that the shared core explains transfer requires interventions (ablation of the core, retraining only the core, or restoring task-specific parameters) to causally link overlap to transfer performance. Without such interventional controls, the observed overlap might be correlated with transferability but not be the mechanism enabling it.

nodes.title: Measured overlap is a set overlap statistic and does not prove functional sufficiency of the shared core

nodes.content:
The quantified bespoke-mask overlap reported (the ~6–10% shared fraction) was computed using bespoke masks obtained with a fixed pruning criterion—typically global unstructured magnitude pruning with rewinding in the intersection experiments—and using a strict all-N intersection threshold (i.e., a parameter is included in the consensus mask only if it remains unpruned in all N bespoke masks); choosing a different pruning criterion for the bespoke masks or relaxing the consensus rule to a k-out-of-N threshold (including parameters retained in at least k of N masks) will change both the size of the intersection and the resulting overlap statistics.
      Fig.5, Fig.12

metadata.failure_mode: If alternative pruning criteria or thresholding strategies produced systematically larger or smaller shared cores, then the specific quantitative claim about a ~6–10% backbone would not generalize; the qualitative conclusion (there exists a small shared core) might persist but the reported magnitude and its practical implications (how much of the model is universal) would be unreliable. The intermediate link that fails is the mapping from one-pruning-rule intersection statistics (Fig. 5, Fig. 12) to a general statement about bespoke-mask overlap across tasks.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper reports overlap numbers for a particular pipeline (global unstructured, rewinding, 2 iterations for N=5 intersection). If other reasonable choices (structured pruning, different per-iteration rates, or k-out-of-N voting) materially change the shared fraction, then the numeric claim (6–10%) is contingent and may not generalize beyond the tested pipeline.

nodes.title: Overlap magnitude depends on pruning rule and intersection threshold

nodes.content:
The empirical claim that intersection-derived prêt-à-porter masks retrain to test accuracies comparable to bespoke masks is evaluated under the fixed retraining protocol used throughout these experiments—stochastic gradient descent for 30 epochs, constant learning rate 0.01, batch size 32—and the paper explicitly states that networks are not trained to full convergence under this recipe; hence similarity in reported test accuracy between intersection-derived and bespoke masks may depend on this limited, non-optimized training regime rather than reflecting their relative performance under fully optimized training.
      Fig.6

metadata.failure_mode: If under longer or tuned training regimes britannique bespoke tickets outperformed intersection tickets (or vice versa), the practical claim that intersection yields trainable high-sparsity tickets "comparable to bespoke tickets" would need to be qualified: parity would be protocol-dependent. The broken step is that Fig. 6's observed accuracy parity would not generalize beyond the limited training budget used in sourcing and retraining experiments.
metadata.weakness_reason: Performance parity reported in Fig. 6 is measured at a particular retraining schedule. If prêt-à-porter and bespoke tickets respond differently to longer training, learning-rate schedules, or augmentation (e.g., bespoke better after tuning), then the observed parity under the chosen protocol may not hold under more realistic or optimized training scenarios; the conclusion about parity would be weaker.

nodes.title: Retraining comparisons use a fixed, non-converged training recipe

nodes.content:
The argument that sourcing N bespoke masks in parallel and then intersecting them yields wall-time savings relative to performing many additional sequential pruning iterations rests on the fact that each bespoke mask can be obtained independently and therefore the elapsed (wall-clock) time to obtain a high-sparsity intersection can be reduced by parallelism; however, the experiments do not report measured wall-clock timings comparing the parallel pipeline to the sequential pipeline, and the paper notes that the parallel pipeline consumes similar total CPU work while saving elapsed time equivalent to avoiding the extra sequential pruning iterations.
      Alg. 1, Fig.12, Fig.6

metadata.failure_mode: If realistic deployment constraints (limited parallel workers, queueing, or significant overheads per run) negate the elapsed-time advantage, then the operational claim that intersection-based sourcing is a practical wall-time speedup would not hold in many settings; the conclusion would reduce to an algorithmic parallelizability observation rather than an empirically demonstrated performance win. The step that breaks is the mapping from theoretical parallelizability to practical speedup in realistic compute environments.
metadata.weakness_reason: Parallelizing independent runs reduces elapsed (calendar) time given access to N workers, but practical wall-clock speedups depend on resource availability, per-run overheads, communication for intersection, and possible differences in per-source-task compute (e.g., sourcing on harder tasks may take longer). Without measured timings, the claimed practical speedups are suggestive but not empirically quantified.

nodes.title: Parallel sourcing shortens elapsed time but wall-clock timings were not measured

nodes.content:
The observation that finetuning a pruned network in place versus rewinding unpruned weights to their initial values prior to the next pruning iteration produces substantially different subsequent masks (with Jaccard distance between the two strategies growing over pruning iterations) was made under a specific experimental finetuning schedule—training/pruning rounds consisting of 30 SGD epochs per round and 20% pruning per iteration—and the magnitude and pattern of the mask divergence reported could depend on how finetuning is implemented in practice (for example, the number of finetuning epochs, the learning rate used during finetuning, whether batch-normalization statistics are updated or frozen during finetuning).
      Fig.9

metadata.failure_mode: If alternate finetuning practices (e.g., smaller LR, longer finetune, freezing some layers) reduced mask divergence versus rewinding, then the conclusion as stated ("substantially alters resulting mask structure") would need to be scoped: the sensitivity to weight-handling would be protocol-dependent and less general. The intermediate link that fails is generalizing the observed Jaccard growth in Fig. 9 to all finetuning variants.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper documents consistent mask-change trends across multiple pruning techniques (Fig. 9), but finetuning is a broad family of interventions; other plausible finetuning choices could yield smaller differences relative to rewinding. If so, the conclusion should be qualified as "under the evaluated finetuning protocol" rather than universally true for all finetuning strategies.

nodes.title: Rewinding vs finetuning divergence depends on finetuning schedule and implementation details

nodes.content:
The ranking of pruning rules by how consistently they identify the same unpruned parameters across tasks (the claim that global unstructured pruning is most consistent, excluding deterministic random baselines) is based in these experiments on the statistic counting how many weights remain unpruned in 0 through 5 of the evaluated tasks (i.e., per-weight counts of how many tasks kept the weight), and this ranking can change if an alternative consistency metric is used (for example, a normalized overlap measure, a per-layer weighted overlap, or other summary statistics) or if deterministic random pruning is treated as a legitimate baseline rather than excluded.
      Fig.12

metadata.failure_mode: If a normalized or functionally-weighted consistency metric reversed the ranking (e.g., some structured rule preserves more task-general channels even if fewer absolute weights), then the conclusion that global unstructured is "most consistent" would be contingent on the chosen metric and less general. The intermediate break is that Fig. 12's raw-count evidence would not translate to a metric-invariant superiority of global unstructured pruning.
metadata.weakness_reason: The paper correctly highlights that random pruning trivially reproduces masks with a fixed seed; excluding those trivial baselines is sensible. However, the practical import of "most consistent" depends on the metric: e.g., global unstructured may retain consistent indices in large layers simply because they have many parameters, biasing counts. Alternate normalized metrics or functional-transfer evaluations could alter the ranking.

nodes.title: Consistency ranking depends on the chosen metric and treatment of random baselines

nodes.content:
The experiments document that parameters retained in prêt-à-porter consensus masks tend to have smaller empirical standard deviation at initialization (averaged per layer and reported in comparison plots) than parameters retained in bespoke masks of similar sparsity, and they report that this property correlates with improved retrainability and training stability under the experimental training recipe; however, no causal intervention (for example, reinitializing or rescaling selected parameters to test whether reducing their initial variance improves learning) is presented, so the relationship is reported as a correlation rather than proven causation.
      Fig.7, Fig.20

metadata.failure_mode: If smaller initialization variance is merely correlated (for example, because intersection tends to pick small-magnitude channels by construction) and not causally responsible for retrainability, then the interpretive claim that prêt-à-porter "concentrate on weights with smaller initial variance, a property linked to improved learnability" would need to be qualified: the link to learnability would be speculative and require direct causal tests. The break is between measured initialization statistics (Fig. 20) and the attribution of improved retrainability to those statistics.
metadata.weakness_reason: The observed correlation is plausible given known effects of initialization scale on training, yet without controlled experiments that alter only initialization variance of the intersected set, one cannot conclude that the intersection procedure succeeds because it selects lower-variance weights rather than because lower-variance is an incidental correlate of being selected by the intersection rule.

nodes.title: Smaller initialization variance correlates with but is not shown to cause better retrainability

nodes.content:
The negative result that most masks do not produce above-random performance at initialization is based on evaluations of bespoke and prêt-à-porter masks applied to the untrained networks prior to any training, using the preprocessing and resizing procedures described for these experiments (images normalized to training statistics and resized to the input dimensions expected by each architecture) and up to six experimental seeds; some runs for certain architecture/dataset pairs are missing due to job-submission issues noted in the experimental appendices, so the initialization evaluation conclusions apply to the reported subset of architectures, datasets, and seeds.
      Fig.21

metadata.failure_mode: If other architectures, initialization schemes, or more exhaustive seed sampling produced more frequent above-random supermask behavior, then the conclusion would be too strong: it would need to be restated as "under the evaluated settings, most tickets do not yield above-random performance at initialization" rather than a broader statement. The broken mapping is from the sampled experimental regime (Fig.21) to a general statement about tickets at initialization.
metadata.weakness_reason: The experiments show a clear pattern for the considered models and data: only larger, highly over-parameterized networks (AlexNet, VGG11) show any nontrivial initial performance. However, missing seeds and the limited model/task families mean the negative finding may not extend to other architectures, initializations, pretraining regimes, or alternative masking/pruning rules; the conclusion should be read as an empirical observation within the explored regime.

nodes.title: Initialization supermask evaluation is limited by architectures, seeds, and some missing runs

nodes.content: Across multiple pruning techniques (global unstructured, L1-unstructured, L2-structured, L1-structured, L_infty-structured, random structured/unstructured) and six experimental seeds, the authors report per-layer and total Jaccard distances that grow with pruning iteration, shown in layer-wise plots and pairwise total-distance heatmaps, indicating robust, reproducible structural divergence among masks produced from the same initialization.

metadata.credit: This element materially strengthens Conclusion 1 because it (a) measures mask structure at multiple granularities (per-layer and total), (b) does so across several independent pruning algorithms rather than a single baseline, and (c) reports consistency across seeds (error bars over six runs). Together these controls preempt the objection that observed differences are a one-off artifact of a single pruning rule or seed: the multiplicity of methods and seed averaging supports the claim that distinct masks routinely arise under plausible algorithmic choices. Without these multi-method, multi-seed measurements (Figs. 3, 4, 10), the assertion of non-uniqueness would rest on much weaker anecdotal evidence.

nodes.title: Multi-method mask divergence documented across layers and iterations

nodes.content: The paper presents accuracy-versus-sparsity curves (Fig. 2 and Appendix Fig. 8) showing that different pruning techniques yield sub-networks with comparable test accuracy at the same sparsity levels across multiple architectures and datasets.

metadata.credit: By demonstrating that structurally different masks reach similar accuracy-sparsity trade-offs, this evidence substantiates the substantive part of Conclusion 1: the masks are not only different sets of indices but also constitute viable trainable solutions (i.e., different "winning" tickets in performance terms). This cross-check reduces the risk that mask differences are irrelevant (e.g., all but one mask being untrainable); it therefore materially supports the interpretation that multiple distinct trainable subnetworks exist within the same initialization/architecture.

nodes.title: Comparable accuracy at similar sparsity across pruning methods

nodes.content: The authors quantify inter-task mask overlap for bespoke tickets (e.g., pairwise Jaccard plots and the specific report of ~6–10% shared retained parameters at ≈99% sparsity in LeNet/AlexNet experiments), showing a measurable nonzero core across diverse task pairs.

metadata.credit: This empirical quantification directly supports Conclusion 2 by providing a concrete numeric statement about the size of the shared backbone; the presence of a reproducible nonzero overlap across architectures and seeds (Fig. 5) rules out the extreme interpretation that bespoke masks are entirely disjoint, and therefore gives weight to the paper's mixed conclusion that masks are largely dissimilar but retain a small consistent core. The quantified overlap is the specific load-bearing evidence that moves the claim from vague ("share something") to concrete ("~6–10% overlap at very high sparsity").

nodes.title: Quantified small shared backbone across tasks at high sparsity

nodes.content: Using N=5 source tasks and sourcing bespoke tickets after two pruning iterations, the paper shows that the intersection mask can reach high sparsity (e.g., ~85% for LeNet) and that these intersection-derived tickets retrain to test accuracies comparable to bespoke tickets of similar sparsity (Fig. 6), evaluated over six seeds.

metadata.credit: This experimental result is the direct operational evidence for Conclusion 3: it demonstrates that the intersection procedure can produce high-sparsity masks that are trainable in practice, not only smaller masks in the abstract. Because retraining parity is shown over multiple seeds and architectures, the evidence guards against the trivial possibility that the intersection only produces smaller but untrainable masks; instead it shows the procedure preserves practical trainability under the evaluated protocol (Fig. 6).

nodes.title: Intersection-based prêt-à-porter tickets retrain to comparable accuracy in experiments

nodes.content: The authors provide an explicit algorithm (Alg. 1) that constructs a consensus mask by independently sourcing bespoke tickets on separate datasets and intersecting their masks; this procedure is, by construction, embarrassingly parallel and was instantiated with N=5 tasks in experiments.

metadata.credit: Alg. 1 gives the concrete mechanism that underwrites the paper's claim about parallelizable sourcing: it shows how independent runs combine into a single intersection mask without inter-run dependence, thereby preempting objections that intersection requires synchronization or sequential dependence. While this does not by itself quantify runtime benefits, it is a load-bearing structural reason to credit the claim that sourcing can be parallelized in principle and was executed as such in the experiments.

nodes.title: Algorithmic parallelizability and explicit consensus procedure (Alg.1)

nodes.content: Figure 9 presents layer-wise Jaccard distances between masks obtained under rewinding and finetuning across multiple pruning techniques and six seeds, showing consistent growth of divergence with pruning iterations and differing patterns between structured and unstructured pruning.

metadata.credit: This controlled, layer-resolved measurement substantiates Conclusion 4: it isolates the effect of weight-handling (rewind vs finetune) on mask evolution and shows the effect is systematic across pruning rules and layers. The layer-level granularity helps rule out a claim that weight-handling only causes negligible, global differences, by demonstrating where (which layers) and how divergence accumulates, strengthening the conclusion's interpretive and reproducibility claims.

nodes.title: Layer-wise Jaccard analysis shows weight-handling sensitivity across pruning methods

nodes.content: Figure 12 reports, per pruning iteration, counts of AlexNet weights that remain unpruned across 0–5 tasks for each pruning technique, and shows that global unstructured pruning yields larger bars in bins corresponding to being kept across many tasks (excluding seeded random pruning which trivially reproduces masks).

metadata.credit: This quantitative, per-iteration tally directly supports Conclusion 5 by providing a concrete consistency metric across tasks and pruning methods: it demonstrates that global unstructured pruning tends to preserve the same parameter indices across multiple tasks more often than the other tested magnitude-based criteria, which explains why intersections derived from global unstructured masks are denser and more useful for prêt-à-porter construction.

nodes.title: Cross-task counts show global unstructured pruning yields more consistent per-weight retention

nodes.content: Figures 7 and 20 present the empirical distributions and layer-wise standard deviations at initialization for (a) the full parameter set, (b) the prêt-à-porter ticket subset, and (c) bespoke ticket subsets across several architectures, showing systematically smaller per-layer empirical standard deviation for the prêt-à-porter-selected weights.

metadata.credit: The explicit layer-wise statistical comparison supplies the central empirical observation for Conclusion 6: the intersection procedure selects parameters whose initialization distribution exhibits lower variance. This measured regularity is non-trivial and supports the interpretive hypothesis that intersection acts as a denoising selection, which plausibly contributes to improved retrainability; without these numerical comparisons the claim about initialization statistics would be speculative.

nodes.title: Layer-wise initialization-variance measurements comparing bespoke and prêt-à-porter tickets

nodes.content: Figure 21 reports test performance of bespoke and prêt-à-porter masks evaluated at initialization (no training) across multiple architectures and target datasets, documenting that only tickets from large, over-parameterized networks (AlexNet, VGG11) show nontrivial above-random performance in this regime.

metadata.credit: This systematic across-architecture measurement is the direct empirical evidence for Conclusion 7: it provides a consistent negative result (no above-random supermask in most cases) with a clear exception pattern, thereby supporting the conclusion's nuanced phrasing. Because the paper reports seeds and notes missing runs, the measurement is transparently presented and guards against overclaiming.

nodes.title: Systematic evaluation of mask performance at initialization across architectures

steps.reasoning: Define a binary mask $\mathbb{M}$ over a network's $D$ parameters $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ as the set of binary indicators $m_i = \mathbf{1}_{\text{unpruned}}(\theta_i)\in\{0,1\}$ that mark whether parameter $\theta_i$ is unpruned; denote $|\mathbb{M}|=D$ as the number of mask entries.

Define the Jaccard distance $d_J(\mathbb{M}_1,\mathbb{M}_2)$ between two masks $\mathbb{M}_1$ and $\mathbb{M}_2$ as $d_J(\mathbb{M}_1,\mathbb{M}_2) = 1 - \frac{|\mathbb{M}_1\cap\mathbb{M}_2|}{|\mathbb{M}_1\cup\mathbb{M}_2|}$, where $|\cdot|$ denotes set cardinality; this quantity measures structural dissimilarity between masks (with $d_J=0$ meaning identical masks and $d_J=1$ meaning disjoint masks).

Describe the experimental setup that produced the evidence: multiple pruning procedures were applied to identical base architectures with identical initializations (the same random seed), using seven pruning techniques that include magnitude-based global unstructured, $L_1$-unstructured, $L_2$-structured, $L_1$-structured, $L_\infty$-structured, random structured, and random unstructured; pruning proceeded iteratively with a fixed per-iteration pruning fraction (20% of remaining connections/units per layer) and weight rewinding to initialization between iterations, and models were trained for 30 epochs before each pruning iteration using SGD with learning rate $0.01$ and batch size $32$ as described in the methodology.

Present the primary observation: per-layer Jaccard distances between masks obtained from one pruning baseline ($L_2$-structured pruning used as a reference) and masks obtained from other pruning techniques increase as pruning iterations proceed; this is evidenced by layer-wise plots showing $d_J$ growing with iteration number, demonstrating masks diverge in structure early and increasingly so as sparsity increases. 
Fig.3

Present the complementary global observation: pairwise total Jaccard distances (aggregated across all parameters) between masks produced by different pruning techniques grow with sparsity and approach maximal dissimilarity as the networks become progressively sparser, indicating little to no overlap among masks found by different pruning methods at high sparsity levels.
Fig.4

Report that the same pattern—early divergence in mask structure and growth of mask dissimilarity with pruning iteration—was observed across multiple base architectures and dataset combinations examined in the paper (for example, additional plots for different architectures and datasets show similar trends), establishing that the result is not an isolated artifact of a single model or dataset.
Fig.2
Fig.10

Record the methodological control that identical initializations (identical seed) were used when comparing pruning methods, so the observed mask dissimilarities cannot be attributed to different random initial weights; therefore, different pruning algorithms applied to the same initialization identify different sparse connectivity patterns rather than trivially differing only in final trained weight values.

Conclude from the empirical observations and controls above that a single initialization and architecture can contain multiple distinct trainable sparse solutions (multiple "winning" lottery tickets) that achieve competitive test accuracy at comparable sparsity levels; these solutions exhibit large structural dissimilarity measured by per-layer and total Jaccard distances that grow with pruning iteration, disproving uniqueness of a single winning mask under different iterative pruning techniques.

Define a bespoke lottery ticket as a mask $\mathbb{M}_i$ obtained by applying the iterative--magnitude-based pruning pipeline (train, prune, rewind) to an identical network initialization but trained on a specific source dataset; thus, "bespoke" denotes task-specific sourcing of a ticket.

Describe the experimental procedure used to compare bespoke masks across tasks: fix a pruning method (e.g., global unstructured pruning), create identical replicas of a model with the same initialization seed, source bespoke masks by training and iteratively pruning each replica on different source datasets drawn from a family of image-classification tasks (for example, MNIST, KMNIST, FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN), and compute pairwise mask overlaps between bespoke masks using the Jaccard distance $d_J$ defined as $d_J(\mathbb{M}_1,\mathbb{M}_2)=1-\frac{|\mathbb{M}_1\cap\mathbb{M}_2|}{|\mathbb{M}_1\cup\mathbb{M}_2|}$.

Report the empirical observation that average pairwise Jaccard distances between bespoke masks sourced on different tasks increase as sparsity increases (as shown in the pairwise total Jaccard distance plots), indicating substantial structural dissimilarity between bespoke masks even for tasks with similar data distributions (for example, CIFAR-10 vs CIFAR-100 or MNIST vs KMNIST).
Fig.5

State the quantitative core-overlap finding: even at very high sparsity (the paper reports examples up to approximately $99\%$ sparsity), bespoke masks are not completely disjoint but retain a small consistent shared backbone; empirically, this shared backbone corresponds to roughly $6\%-10\%$ overlap of unpruned parameters across tasks in the experiments reported, i.e., $|\bigcap_i \mathbb{M}_i|/|\mathbb{M}_i|\approx 0.06\text{--}0.10$ in the high-sparsity regime.
Fig.5

Explain the inferential consequence: because bespoke masks are, on average, substantially structurally dissimilar but still share a small consistent core, the transferability of tickets across tasks cannot be trivially explained by near-identity of full masks; instead, transfer may be supported by this small shared backbone together with task-specific variations.

State upstream results treated as established: (a) bespoke masks sourced on different tasks are, on average, substantially dissimilar but share a small consistent core (conclusion 2); (b) global unstructured magnitude pruning is the most consistent magnitude-based pruning rule across tasks (conclusion 5). These results are used as premises for the prêt-à-porter construction and its evaluation.

Define the prêt-à-porter consensus construction: given $N$ bespoke binary masks $\mathbb{M}_1,\mathbb{M}_2,\dots,\mathbb{M}_N$ obtained from identical initializations but trained on different source tasks, compute the consensus mask $\mathbb{M} = \bigcap_{i=1}^N \mathbb{M}_i$, i.e., perform an element-wise logical AND so that an entry is unpruned in $\mathbb{M}$ only if it is unpruned in every bespoke mask; note that a relaxed threshold (e.g., requiring unpruned in $k$ out of $N$) is also possible but the paper focuses on full intersection.

Explain the computational advantage: because each bespoke ticket $\mathbb{M}_i$ is sourced independently on a separate task and the masks are obtained by running the iterative pruning pipeline on independent replicas, the sourcing of the $N$ bespoke tickets can be executed embarrassingly parallel across machines; after all bespoke masks are computed the intersection is a single, inexpensive element-wise operation, thus enabling wall-time speedups relative to running many sequential pruning iterations on a single replica.

Describe the experimental instantiation used to evaluate prêt-à-porter tickets: choose $N=5$ source tasks (MNIST, FashionMNIST, KMNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN) that share output dimensionality $k=10$ and compatible input sizes; use identical initializations (same seed) for each replica; source bespoke tickets by applying global unstructured pruning with rewinding for $T=2$ pruning iterations with per-iteration pruning fraction $t=0.2$ (so each bespoke ticket is relatively low-to-moderate sparsity; for LeNet this produced a bespoke ticket of $\approx 35.9\%$ sparsity after two iterations); compute the consensus mask $\mathbb{M}=\bigcap_{i=1}^5\mathbb{M}_i$ and set the remaining weights to their initial values.
Fig.1

Report the sparsity and retraining results observed: for LeNet, intersecting the five bespoke masks obtained after two pruning iterations produced a prêt-à-porter mask with sparsity approximately $\sim85\%$, which the authors note is comparable to the sparsity of a bespoke ticket obtained after nine sequential pruning iterations; more generally, the intersection produced high-sparsity consensus masks that, when retrained from the initial values of their remaining weights, achieved test accuracies comparable to bespoke tickets of similar sparsity across the evaluated architectures and target tasks.
Fig.6
Fig.12

Explain the interpretive rationale provided: because bespoke masks are noisy and task-specific, taking their intersection acts as a denoising operation that preserves only parameters consistently judged important across multiple tasks; the resulting consensus mask captures a shared core of parameters plausibly associated with broadly useful pathways, which helps explain why the prêt-à-porter mask remains trainable despite its higher sparsity and why intersection-based sparsification can rival many additional sequential pruning iterations.

Report the practical wall-time speedup claim: by sourcing the $N=5$ bespoke tickets in parallel after only two pruning iterations and then intersecting them, the authors effectively save the wall-clock time that would have been spent carrying out the additional seven sequential pruning iterations on one replica (the difference between two and nine iterations), while achieving a mask with similar sparsity and comparable retraining performance; the authors note that this saves elapsed real time but not total CPU work (because the parallel jobs still require CPU on multiple machines).
Fig.1

Conclude that the intersection-based, parallelizable "prêt-à-porter" ticket construction yields trainable, high-sparsity sub-networks whose retraining accuracy is comparable to bespoke tickets of similar sparsity, and that the sourcing stage of this procedure is embarrassingly parallelizable, thereby addressing the sequential bottleneck of many iterative pruning iterations.

Define the two post-pruning weight-handling strategies compared: "rewinding" means that after pruning the remaining (unpruned) weights are reset to their initial (or early checkpoint) values before the next training/pruning iteration; "finetuning" means that after pruning, the remaining weights continue training from their current post-pruning values without rewinding.

Describe the experimental comparison: for identical pruning techniques and identical initializations (same seed), the authors applied both weight-handling strategies (rewinding vs finetuning) across pruning iterations and measured structural differences between the masks that result from the two workflows by computing layer-wise Jaccard distances between masks obtained under the two strategies.

Report the empirical finding that finetuning yields masks that are significantly different from those produced under rewinding across all pruning techniques tested, with the divergence (quantified by Jaccard distance between the two strategies) growing as pruning progresses; specifically, magnitude-based structured pruning shows a Jaccard divergence that grows approximately logarithmically with pruning iterations, whereas magnitude-based unstructured pruning exhibits more complex, layer-dependent divergence trends.
Fig.9

State the methodological implication recorded by the authors: the choice of weight-handling protocol (rewind vs finetune) materially changes the connectivity structure of final masks, which affects reproducibility and interpretation of which connections the pruning protocol deems "important."

Define global unstructured pruning precisely as used in the experiments: given the set of unpruned parameters in a group of layers represented by a tensor $\mathbf{U}$, global unstructured pruning removes the entries $\{U_k : k_{\mathrm{th} }(\{U_i\}_{i=1}^{|\mathbf{U}|}\mid\|\cdot\|_1) < t\}$, where $k_{\mathrm{th}}(\cdot\mid\|\cdot\|_1)$ denotes ranking by $L_1$-norm magnitude and $t=0.2$ is the per-iteration pruning fraction used in the paper's experiments.

Describe the consistency measurement used across tasks: for a given pruning technique, the authors counted, at each pruning iteration, how many weights remained unpruned in 0 through $N$ of the chosen tasks (here $N=5$ tasks: MNIST, FashionMNIST, KMNIST, CIFAR-10, SVHN) for identical initializations; this produces histograms indicating how many parameters are consistently retained across multiple tasks.

Report the empirical observation shown in the consensus histograms: among the tested pruning rules (including $L_2$-structured, global unstructured, $L_1$-unstructured, $L_\infty$-structured, random structured, random unstructured), the global unstructured magnitude-based pruning technique produced the most consistent identification of similar unpruned parameters across the evaluated image-classification tasks — i.e., weights tend to remain unpruned in the same fraction of tasks more often under global unstructured pruning than under other magnitude-based structured criteria.
Fig.12

Explain the qualification regarding random pruning: random structured and random unstructured pruning trivially reproduce the same mask across tasks when the random seed is fixed (because the randomness, not the task, determines which weights are pruned); excluding these deterministic random baselines, global unstructured pruning is the most consistent magnitude-based criterion in producing similar per-weight retention across tasks.

Treat as given the prêt-à-porter construction and empirical retrainability results (conclusion 3): the intersection mask $\mathbb{M}=\bigcap_{i=1}^N\mathbb{M}_i$ produces a high-sparsity, trainable sub-network when sourced from $N$ bespoke tickets; this is taken as an established starting point for the present analysis of initialization statistics.

Define the statistic used to compare initialization distributions: for each layer, compute the empirical standard deviation (sample standard deviation) of the initial values of all parameters in that layer, and likewise compute the empirical standard deviation of initial values restricted to the subset of parameters that comprise a mask (e.g., the prêt-à-porter mask or a bespoke mask); denote the layer-wise empirical standard deviation of the full initialization as $\sigma_{\text{full,layer}}$ and of a masked subset as $\sigma_{\text{mask,layer}}$.

Report the empirical observation for AlexNet (and analogous observations for other architectures reported in appendices): the distribution of initial values of parameters that survive into the prêt-à-porter mask shows a stronger tendency toward smaller magnitude and a smaller empirical standard deviation per layer compared to the initial distributions of parameters that survive into bespoke tickets of similar sparsity; visually, the histogram of initial weight values for the prêt-à-porter ticket is more concentrated and closer to the full initialization distribution than bespoke-ticket histograms.
Fig.7
Fig.17

Report the aggregated, layer-wise quantification: for each architecture examined (ResNet18, AlexNet, LeNet, VGG11), compute and plot the average empirical standard deviation per layer for (a) the full initial weight distribution, (b) the prêt-à-porter ticket subset, (c) a CIFAR-10 bespoke ticket subset, and (d) a MNIST bespoke ticket subset; these plots show that $\sigma_{\text{prêt-à-porter,layer}}$ is generally lower than $\sigma_{\text{bespoke,layer}}$ and closer to $\sigma_{\text{full,layer}}$ across layers.
Fig.20

Relate initialization variance to learnability as stated by the authors: the authors note that the scale (standard deviation) of initial weights is known to be important for training stability, and they empirically observe that prêt-à-porter tickets' concentration on weights with smaller initial variance correlates with improved retrainability and training stability in the experiments (i.e., the prêt-à-porter LTs retrain reliably to comparable test accuracies while exhibiting initialization statistics closer to the original initialization).
Fig.6

Record the authors' interpretive claim (as presented without formal proof): intersecting bespoke masks acts as a denoising operation that preferentially selects parameters whose initial values are closer to the canonical initialization distribution (i.e., smaller empirical standard deviation), and this selection is plausibly linked to the observed improved learnability of the resulting prêt-à-porter tickets; the paper frames this as an empirical correlation rather than a proven causal mechanism.

Define the evaluation performed "at initialization": take a binary mask (bespoke or prêt-à-porter), apply it to the network at its random initialization (i.e., zero-out pruned parameters and leave unpruned parameters at their initial values) and measure test-set accuracy of the resulting masked, untrained network; this measures "supermask" performance prior to any training.

Describe the empirical test set used and architectures evaluated for initialization performance: the paper evaluated masked initial networks across multiple architecture-dataset combinations including LeNet, AlexNet, VGG11, and ResNet18 on datasets such as MNIST, FashionMNIST, KMNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and EMNIST.

Report the empirical result: for most evaluated architecture-task combinations, neither bespoke nor prêt-à-porter tickets produced better-than-random test performance at initialization; the only exceptions observed were bespoke tickets sourced on large, highly over-parameterized architectures such as AlexNet and VGG11, which exhibited non-trivial initial performance (i.e., above random baseline).
Fig.21

Record the inferential conclusion stated by the authors: therefore, for most tested models and datasets the trainability advantage of tickets manifests only after training rather than being present as a strong "supermask" at initialization; nontrivial supermask performance at initialization appears to be an exception limited to large, parameter-inefficient architectures in the experiments reported.

open_questions.content: Several scientifically meaningful questions remain open or are acknowledged limitations of the present empirical study. First, the mechanistic explanation for lottery-ticket transferability is unresolved: although bespoke masks share a small consistent core and tickets can be retrained across related tasks, the underlying reasons why those shared parameters suffice for transfer (e.g., whether they implement generic feature extractors, preserve information pathways, or bias optimization) are not characterized. Second, scalability and robustness remain open: prior work and this study note difficulties in producing trainable small sparse tickets in larger models and datasets (e.g., ResNet-50 or ImageNet-scale tasks), and it is not established whether the consensus intersection approach generalizes to those large-scale regimes without further methodological adaptation. Third, sensitivity to training protocol and hyperparameters is a limitation: failures observed on some datasets (for example, SVHN in these experiments) indicate that dataset-specific training recipes or optimizer schedules can materially affect ticket retrainability, and the optimal training regimes for consensus-derived tickets have not been determined. Fourth, methodological design choices in consensus construction are unresolved: how many and which source tasks to include, what threshold of agreement (intersection vs. k-out-of-N voting) yields the best trade-off between sparsity and generality, and how to choose the pruning rule used to source bespoke tickets for intersection are open empirical questions. Finally, a theoretical characterization of what distinguishes a lottery ticket mask from other sub-networks (beyond empirical measures of retrainability and mask overlap) is missing; developing principled importance definitions and analytic explanations for the observed mask structure and variance properties is left for future theoretical work.
